notes.meaning: Ezekiel's guide now takes him out of the temple building and into the court on the north side. There he sees a block of rooms set across from the open area behind the temple. Matthew Henry notes that these private rooms stood right beside the place of public worship. He sees in this a reminder that going to church does not replace praying to God alone at home.

The block of rooms was a hundred cubits long and fifty wide, with its door on the north. A cubit is about a forearm's length. Its long side matched the hundred-cubit open area behind the temple. Ezekiel had already been told about rooms for the priests, and now he looks at them more closely.

The building had galleries, which are open walkways along the upper floors. One side faced the inner court. The other side faced the paved area of the outer court. Wesley pictures the rooms sitting between these galleries, back to back.

In front of the rooms ran a walkway ten cubits wide. The doors opened north onto it, so people could step straight from the walk into the rooms. Matthew Henry sees these walks as places where people could meet and talk and help one another grow in faith. Christians are made for fellowship, not only for church and private prayer.

The building had three floors. It had no pillars to hold up the upper galleries, so each upper floor was set back and the top rooms were smaller. Wesley thinks the rooms also got lower in height as they went up. Matthew Henry and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note how many rooms there were. They link this to Jesus' words, "In my Father's house are many mansions" (John 14:2). There is room for all who come to God.

An outer wall fifty cubits long stood in front of the rooms. It ran toward the outer court. The rooms on the outer court side were fifty cubits long, while the side facing the temple was a hundred cubits long. Keil & Delitzsch think this wall stood along the short east end of the building. It may have shielded the lower windows from view while the priests changed their clothes.
The way into these rooms came from the east, from the outer court. Seen from that side, the rooms seemed to rise up from behind the wall. The way in did not come from the inner court.

A second block of rooms stood on the south side, across from the open area behind the temple. It was built just like the one on the north. It had the same length and width, the same walkway, the same doors and the same exits. Wesley says it was exactly alike in every way.

Now the guide explains what the rooms are for. They are holy rooms where the priests eat the "most holy" offerings. These were the parts of the grain, sin and guilt offerings that were not burned on the altar. The priests ate them as God's servants, and no one else could share them. The food was also kept there until it was cooked and eaten. Matthew Henry notes that eating in a holy place set these meals apart from ordinary meals.

The priests wore special holy clothes while they served at the altar. They had to leave those clothes in these rooms and put on ordinary clothes before going out among the people. Matthew Henry says this kept the holy garments clean and showed honor for the service. The priests then went out in common clothes to teach the people and answer their questions.

With the inside of the temple area fully measured, the guide leads Ezekiel out through the east gate. Then he measures the whole area all around. Matthew Henry says we now see how far this holy ground reaches.

The east side measures five hundred. The Hebrew text says five hundred rods (or "reeds"), not cubits. A rod was about six cubits, so each side would be more than a mile long, an area bigger than all of old Jerusalem. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says this huge size shows the temple is a picture of something greater. It points to the great growth of God's kingdom.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars follow the ancient Greek translation, which reads "cubits" instead of "rods." On that reading, this is simply the outer wall of the temple courts, five hundred cubits on each side. Many modern Bibles, like the BSB, read it this way.

notes.meaning: The guide measures the north, south and west sides in the same way. Each is five hundred long, making a perfect square. Matthew Henry and Wesley see this great size as a picture of the church in the gospel age. It is wide enough to take in people from every nation. They say this is partly fulfilled already as non-Jewish people come to Christ, and will be fully fulfilled when "all Israel shall be saved."

A wall ran all the way around the square to keep the holy apart from the common. Matthew Henry draws a lesson from this. We should treat God's name, God's day and God's Word as different from ordinary things, and come to worship with a pause and respect. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that this wall no longer splits Jew from non-Jew (Ephesians 2:14). It only separates holy from unholy. Its square shape pictures a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
